newsitem.title: INDIA: Glimmer of hope in India, Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: Glimmer of hope in India, Pakistan talks.

text.p: After 50 years of strained relations, India and Pakistan have made a promising start to a new peace process that offers hope of an eventual easing of tensions in volatile South Asia.
Indian officials and analysts said the two neighbours have embarked on a new approach in negotiations after a three-year break stained by acrimony and a revolt in Kashmir.
"For the first time, there is a glimmer of a possibility of a certain amount of acceptable peace returning," a government official close to the talks said.

The two rounds of talks between high-level foreign ministry officials have set a deliberate, step-by-step pace to the sensitive negotiations, which is considered significant as it minimises the risk that negotiations will snag on thorny issues such as Kashmir.

Officials said the two countries' foreign secretaries -- the highest ranking civil servants in the foreign ministries -- were expected to hold a third round in early May before their prime ministers meet on the margins of a regional summit in the Maldives on May 12-14.
The approach is seen increasing the chances for agreement on less contentious issues, leaving the most difficult problems until later.
But it virtually ensures that the process, which is vulnerable to political winds on either side of the border, will be a drawn-out one, they said.
As Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral recently said: "A refrigerator needs time to defreeze."
"For 50 years they have not found solutions," said Jasjit Singh, head of the government-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses. "Surely it will take time."

On Wednesday, Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, held their first talks as ministers. As a goodwill gesture, they quickly agreed to free several hundred fishermen held by the two countries.
Officials said the two sides were expected to release civilian prisoners at a later date as part of an effort to address humanitarian issues.
Gujral has said he is keen to promote contact between citizens of the two nations in order to build confidence.
Last month, India unilaterally relaxed visa restrictions for Pakistani businessmen and journalists, and said Pakistani tourist groups would be allowed to visit India.

Khan has stressed the benefits of greater trade and commerce, citing a pipeline from Turkmenistan which could supply India with oil, and electricity for power-starved northern India from Pakistan's hydroelectric facilities.

The step-by-step approach marks a shift in Pakistan's policy. In talks which broke down in early 1994, Islamabad had insisted the two sides make progress in settling their half-century-old dispute over the Kashmir region before tackling other, less difficult issues.
Pakistan still considers Kashmir to be the central issue, but is willing to deal with the matter's various aspects separately while simultaneously taking up unrelated issues.
"The core issue is Kashmir, and as I have suggested, that can be dealt with in a step-by-step manner and a lot can be solved," Khan told reporters earlier this week.

Khan suggested India reduce its security forces in its two-thirds of Kashmir. But Indian officials said they were heartened when he appeared to concede that troops were needed there partly because of cross-border infiltration by militants.
Indian officials said the substance of talks remained difficult, but the two rounds of negotiations had so far been free of tension.

"The talks have been remarkably free of acrimony or ire of any kind," a senior official said, noting that in 1993 when Khan was speaker of Pakistan's lower house of parliament, he had made controversial remarks about India during a visit to Delhi.
"This time he was warm, available and friendly," the official said.

Khan said on Tuesday: "In 50 years we have ended up fighting three times. Who gained from that? Probably those who make the weapons and their agents who get the commissions. Neither India nor Pakistan gained anything out of this."
